sections.title: Psychological concepts: potentially helpful, but not true
Therapeutic techniques: helpful inside a relationship

toc.title: How the concepts connect to Polyvagal Theory

blocks.p: It's just you. The psychological concepts you hear about all the time, the ego, the shadow, the parts, the inner child, are not actually real in reality. They're ideas. Here I want to be more clear and more structured about how I think about all of this, and how it connects to Polyvagal Theory. And I'm going to give you my own brand new psychological concept, too.
This started with a letter from a student in my Polyvagal 101 course. They wrote:

"I got through the first part of the course, but I'm a little confused. I have a limited understanding of psychology, or whatever the proper term is, and I'm getting caught up in how all these systems and ideas fit or don't fit together."

Yes, this stuff is confusing. It's very confusing. What they're referring to is that there are other psychological concepts, and modalities, that just kind of float around. They're there. Concepts of reparenting, concepts of ego, concepts of having parts or child parts. Shadow work, shadow self, true self, authentic self. I'm going to call these psychological concepts. These things don't actually exist. They're not real. They're ideas that come from the soft science of psychology.

Polyvagal Theory is different. I, as a therapist, do not lay claim to Polyvagal Theory. It crosses professions. It's biology. It's not specific to the field of psychology, and it's not specific to the practice of therapy. It's science, and it's the foundation to other professions, so it can be incorporated into them.

So the question becomes: how do these other psychological ideas connect to Polyvagal Theory? How does the science of the autonomic nervous system, the science of mammalian connection, the science of defense, connect to things like ego and shadow self? Where's the intersection? That's a really big question.
They went on:

"I'm looking to take courses like yours, but I'm reaching information overload. I've been studying attachment theory, abandonment issues, been doing CBT and EMDR in therapy, and I've heard about inner child healing, shadow work, somatic therapy, and I'm sure there are hundreds of ideas I have not come across yet."

You're absolutely correct. There are many, many ideas that come from the field of psychology and the practice of therapy, and they don't necessarily build on each other or have a clear intersection. I think all of them, as a group, do have an intersection with Polyvagal Theory. I'll get to that.

blocks.why: This article is about practicing. This is the practice built from your check-ins.

blocks.p: Having so many ideas is a problem, and it's also not a problem. I think competition is good. Having competing ideas is a good thing. But as consumers, as potential clients in therapy, we need to search for what clicks within us.

It's tricky, because I don't expect the layperson to be able to tell who is a valid expert and who's not. We're not all valid. As human beings we are, but our ideas are not all valid. Our ideas are not all substantiated, and they may not work for everybody. I'm going to have some opinions here that don't work for everybody. I may be an expert on some level, but that doesn't mean my ideas will click with you.

So I'd really encourage you to identify what clicks for you: what person, what personality, and what ideas just kind of have a pull. Rather than assuming every expert out there has valid ideas and then trying to make them all work. It's completely okay to say yes to some things and no to other things.

blocks.h: Why these concepts don't click for me

blocks.p: Personally, I'm not interested in these psychological concepts. Parts work does not interest me, personally or as a therapist. Reparenting doesn't really interest me. Shadow work, ego work, nothing happens within me. If anything, I'm maybe a little irritated by these ideas.

I think they take us one step away from our true inner felt sense experience. To me, they add a cognitive layer that generally isn't necessary. At the same time, for many people, they absolutely can work. Having these concepts may act as a container for their dysregulated autonomic state. So rather than being in constant panic, they have the concept that a part of me feels this way and a part of me feels another way.

That idea by itself is not a problem for me at all. That's how I work in therapy a lot: we do have somatic feelings, sensations, and experiences, and they can interact. But then to say one of them is a firefighter and one of them is a child, that's where I think we don't need that extra layer of cognition in general. For some people, though, it may actually help contain whatever pain they're going through, the dysregulation they have going on inside of them.

I wouldn't search out someone who thinks in these ways. It wouldn't help me. A coach I was working with brought up shadow work, and I don't know if she noticed, but I kind of rolled my eyes. Get me a step closer to what I'm missing. Get me a step closer to my true felt sense in that moment. That's what I'm looking for.

Same with modalities. I'm personally not very interested in EMDR, or in CBT. Something like Somatic Experiencing interests me a lot more, because it gets me closer to my direct felt experience in that moment. That's just me, and it has no reflection on anyone's success rate. It just doesn't pique my interest.

blocks.h: What actually works: the therapeutic alliance

blocks.p: When you're looking at modalities, keep in mind that what works is not the specific technique. What truly works is the therapeutic alliance. That's the heart and soul of therapy. If that's not there, things like bilateral stimulation are not going to go very far.

Take the therapist out of it altogether. Do you think bilateral stimulation through an app would be helpful? I don't think so. You have to have the co-regulative piece. You have to have that trusting, safe relationship with a therapist for the other techniques to be helpful.
The student also wrote:
"I've been diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety, CPTSD, depression, but like you mentioned in the podcast, I'm not even sure if the diagnostics are really that meaningful or even accurate."

I don't place a whole lot of stock in diagnosis. When someone tells me they've been diagnosed with something, I say, "Okay, help me understand." People self-diagnose way too much, but that's a whole other thing. Even when another therapist diagnoses, I need to know why. I need to know what they're seeing, because I may see something completely different. There are some diagnoses I don't even use. At the time, the places I worked didn't require me to diagnose, and I really liked that. In my private practice, I didn't diagnose. I didn't see the function of it for the work I was doing.

There is a function to it professionally, as a communication tool between professionals. But that's not what we're talking about. As far as Polyvagal Theory is concerned, we can understand these "disorders" as a dysregulated person: a dysregulated autonomic state, and how that shows up through cognitions, behaviors, and behavioral adaptations. In the lack of sociability, we can see that the client in front of us is in a dysregulated, stuck state, not a disorder that is somehow just there.

And if you've ever been part of a treatment team, you probably know people disagree regularly about diagnosis. Two therapists can see the same behaviors, the same history, the same context, and come up with different diagnoses. A psychiatrist and a therapist looking at the same context will come up with different diagnoses. I've been on treatment teams with a psychiatrist, a therapist, a family therapist, someone doing parenting skills, a nurse case manager. Maybe only a couple of them do the formal diagnosis, but a whole bunch of people have different thoughts on what it should be, all based on the same criteria. It's supposed to be objective, but in reality it's just not. I think there are some serious issues with diagnosing.
Then came the big question: "Is Polyvagal the best place to direct my energy? Are there other theories or resources that you think are essential to learn in congruence?"
I break this down into four domains:

In my opinion, Polyvagal Theory is foundational knowledge. It's extremely essential. It really helps to define the experience of being human, or a mammal. I think it even gets us closer to understanding consciousness, or the shifts in what feels like consciousness. That's something I've played around with but I'm not ready to talk about yet, and I haven't even defined what consciousness is.

It helps us understand danger and our reactions to danger. It helps us understand our connections and disconnections. I think that's far more important than learning psychological concepts about ego and reparenting and parts work. This knowledge gets to the heart of who we are. It's normalizing, it's validating. It's a new narrative, but it's also a deeper explanation, and it's something we can build on. Especially when you bring in the Polyvagal ladder, which is a metaphor for the biology. That gives you a roadmap: an idea of what's going to come next, and maybe even what you could do next.

So in my opinion, that's the starting point, for doing your own work, and for therapists in how we conceive of and deliver our services. Do you understand Polyvagal Theory? Do you understand how it connects to trauma? To me, that's absolutely essential.

Understanding things like attachment and abandonment is important. It can be very helpful for gaining insight and understanding, and for reducing judgment and shame. Just having a new narrative, a new understanding, can be very helpful, and learning about attachment can be very helpful to apply to your own life.

I don't think it's enough on its own, and I don't know that it's as important as understanding Polyvagal Theory. Part of understanding Polyvagal Theory blends easily into attachment through co-regulation anyway. But attachment alone doesn't address a stuck autonomic nervous system. It doesn't address why you may have difficulty connecting with people. It kind of does, but Polyvagal Theory takes it a step further, and I think it's foundational to a deeper understanding of attachment.

blocks.h3: Psychological concepts: potentially helpful, but not true

blocks.p: Understanding psychological concepts is potentially helpful, but less important, because these things are not true. There is no shadow self. That's not real. It's a psychological concept. You don't have other parts. That's not true.

I want to be clear: when I say there are no parts within you, I'm not referring to dissociative identity disorder. I'm referring in general to the phenomenon of parts work, which is very, very popular right now.
There's no such thing as an ego. It's a concept, an idea from the field of psychology. And honestly, if you asked various professionals to define it, they'd probably all sound different.

But you can take these concepts and apply them to yourself, and they can act as a metaphor or a reframe that helps reduce the intensity of a dysregulated state. So they have a function. They're ideas we tell ourselves, a top-down narrative, and having a new narrative, even through a metaphor, can be helpful. I don't think it's essential, and it's definitely not enough by itself.

blocks.h3: Therapeutic techniques: helpful inside a relationship

blocks.p: Specific therapeutic techniques are important, but like I said, not as important as the therapeutic alliance. Techniques do help, absolutely. I have a grab bag of things I go to very often. But without a good enough therapeutic alliance with my clients, I don't think they'd be helpful.

Cognitive reframes can be very helpful. That's a CBT technique. Talking to an empty chair can be helpful. Reality testing, practicing listening and communication skills, maybe even bilateral stimulation: all of these and a ton more can be helpful, but they're not sufficient on their own. They have to be done in the context of a solid therapeutic alliance. Otherwise you're basically left with a workbook. I don't think these techniques are powerful enough to really be delivered through an app or a workbook. It could be kind of helpful, sure, but not having a therapeutic alliance would be detrimental.

blocks.h: How the concepts connect to Polyvagal Theory

blocks.p: The student asked a really important question: "Are these other ideas in conflict with the Polyvagal Theory?"

No, I don't think they conflict. The question is how they connect. These are mostly top-down reframes, narratives, and metaphors that can help contain a dysregulated state. So they can help with state regulation. It's a top-down signal, from the big brain to the brainstem: we can understand this, this makes sense. To me, that's the deepest it goes.

Maybe having that reframe, that metaphor, can help you get to the true experience you're going through. Maybe thinking about yourself as different parts helps you actually feel what those different parts feel like in your body. But in reality, there are no other parts. It's a top-down reframe, a new narrative, an idea, a metaphor. There is no shadow state. There are no parts states, as far as I know, for the different internal family members. That's not a thing. It may get you closer to your state by regulating you enough to look inward. It may act as a container that allows you to look inward.

What disinterests me is that it's an added cognitive layer, and on top of that, it relies on an expert who is giving wisdom. An expert who has a breakthrough: "I've discovered this thing about shadow selves, and parts and egos and child selves and true selves and authentic selves. Let me bestow my wisdom." Because no one's finding this stuff in a lab. There's no blood test for your parts. There's no urine test for ego. These are concepts. They are made up.
I'll make one up right now. You heard it here first. It came out of a real therapy session, and there's even a therapeutic modality. We're calling it puzzle completion therapy.

The idea is that you have a completed puzzle self, and you're just missing a piece, maybe two. You're just missing a puzzle piece to become your completed, authentic puzzle self. So you need to identify where the missing piece is inside of you. It's in there somewhere. If you do a body scan, you might notice: there's a piece here where something's missing. Maybe it feels like a pain, or an emptiness, a void.

In puzzle completion therapy, we don't go straight at the pain, or the feeling of emptiness, because that could be too much. It's not the first thing we'd address. Instead, just like a puzzle, we address the outside edges. When you do a puzzle, you start on the outside, right? That's the easiest. That's where you can do the most in the shortest amount of time. You start on the edges and gradually work your way in.

In the real session, I was talking with a teenager who didn't want to focus on the inner pain quite yet. We agreed: let's work on the things that might be easier. Let's focus on getting schoolwork done. So in puzzle completion therapy, that's what we'd do. We'd focus on the outside stuff, the more manageable things, like a sleep schedule or diet. These are challenging, I know. So we'd figure out which ones are most manageable, begin on that outside edge, and then work our way toward the middle pieces: the trauma, the stuck defensive state directly, the attachments and abandonments.
Of course, this wouldn't be limited to therapy. I'd need a coaching component, too, so puzzle completion therapy will be available for coaching soon. We'll call it puzzle completion coaching, PCC.

There you go. A brand new psychological concept, along with a therapeutic modality. It sounds like something, right? Close enough. The scary thing is, if I hadn't obviously made this up and had really fleshed it out, I think I could sell it. I think people would say, "Oh, there is a puzzle piece missing, and it exactly fits what I'm going through." I personally don't see how that's less plausible than saying there's some sort of shadow self. That's just me. If you want to learn more about puzzle completion therapy, let me know, and I'll have to make something up for you.
The student asked, "Is Polyvagal the best place to start, or are there other things I need to master before or alongside?"

I think Polyvagal Theory is extremely important foundational knowledge, and a great place to start if you're asking, "Why am I like this?" and you're ready for new information. When clients ask me why, I say, "Hey, I've got an answer for you." If they're not asking that, if they don't want to learn about biology, and they just want to stay in their thoughts, or get closer to their somatic feelings without spending time learning about the autonomic nervous system, I don't blame them. That's okay.

After that, or along with it, I'd go to somatic focused things. But really, we want things that are comprehensive of thoughts, feelings, sensations, and maybe even more than that. Maybe even spirituality, if that's your thing. We're a whole person, and all of these connect. So if you go the somatic route, don't just look for dancing and singing and breathing. Those are all really important and helpful, but there's a lot more that goes along with them. Somatic Experiencing is something I've spent some time looking into. It seems fantastic. If I were going to go back to school and be certified in anything, that would probably be it.

My recommendation is to learn Polyvagal Theory first. Then, if you're doing self-work, ground yourself in your safety state. Don't go directly at the pain, the stuck defensive state. I don't think it's helpful to go right at it. I think it's more helpful to ground yourself in safety first.

The letter ended: "Honestly, I'm just really overwhelmed, and heard you give a little pushback on inner child work on the podcast. I feel really behind, and it seems that Polyvagal is the best place to start, but I feel like I'm dipping my toes into a little bit of everything and not really retaining a lot of info. I just worry I don't know how any of this works."

I don't blame you. It's totally overwhelming, and I don't think you're the only person who feels that way. Inner child work can be helpful. I'm personally not really into it. But these are concepts. They're made up. Just like my puzzle thing: it's not a real thing. You don't actually have puzzle pieces missing inside of you, but maybe it feels like that, and maybe that would appeal to you.

So here's how it fits together. Polyvagal Theory is the underlying foundational knowledge, the science of how we are the way we are. Learning about things like attachment is extremely helpful knowledge. Psychological concepts can be very useful, but they're metaphors, made-up narratives that can help as a top-down avenue for state regulation. These things don't necessarily conflict.

I want to be more transparent about this stuff, and I think there may be some pushback. Saying "this is made up" probably won't help my relationships with my peers, and neither will pushing back on diagnosis. I don't think the same way as everybody. Rather than tiptoeing, I feel like I need to be transparent. If that works for you, awesome. If it doesn't, that's okay too.
